heading: What I already know about you
intro: You clicked nothing. You accepted no banner, granted no permission, and no cookie was set. This page still opened knowing a few things. They're worth looking at — not because this site is creepy, but because the next one you open can do all of it too, and won't tell you.

history.heading: what I knew before you scrolled
history.lede: None of this came from your browser. It came from this site's own visit history — the same history the home page greets you with. Every one of these is true right now:
history.empty: I couldn't load this visit's history yet.
history.note: The home page picks one of these at a time, the least likely one that happens to be true, and a reload moves to the next. Here they all are at once.

fact.firstEver: You're the first person ever to open this page.
fact.firstFromCity: You're the first person from {{city}} ever to open this page.
fact.firstFromCityInDays: You're the first person from {{city}} in {{days}} days.
fact.milestone: You're exactly the {{position}} person to open this page.
fact.recent24h: You're the {{position}} person here in the last 24 hours.
fact.previous: The last person before you arrived from {{previousCity}}, {{when}}.
fact.position: You're the {{position}} person to open this page.

signals.heading: what your browser volunteered
signals.lede: These are straight reads of public properties. Not one of them triggers a permission prompt, which is exactly why no site has to mention it is reading them:
signals.note: A private window would change none of this. Every reading above works exactly the same in one — that anonymity is from your own history, not from the site.

rarity.heading: how rare that makes you
rarity.lede: Each item on its own is common. Watch what happens as they multiply:
rarity.total: All together: roughly 1 in {{value}} browsers look like yours — {{bits}} bits of entropy. None of it used a cookie.
rarity.caveat: About the arithmetic: only the row marked as measured comes from this site's real data. The rest are rounded slices of published market share, and the multiplication assumes the dimensions are independent — they aren't, language and time zone travel together. So this number overstates you. The uncomfortable part is that overstating barely matters: tracking doesn't need to be accurate, it needs to be consistent. If your browser gets something wrong the same way every time, the mistake becomes part of your identity.

kept.summary: For comparison: what's left of this visit is a country, a city, an approximate coordinate, and a timestamp. No IP — not because it was scrubbed, but because the event that crosses this system has no field for one. And this page stored nothing about you: no cookie, and in browser storage only your language preference. That fingerprint was computed for you to look at and thrown away — check in devtools.

outro: None of this is sophisticated. It's the floor of what any page can do, and most do — except they also store it, join it to third-party cookies, and sell the result in an auction that takes a tenth of a second. The part worth minding isn't that this much is knowable. It's that nobody is obliged to tell you.

auction.heading: what you're worth, and what they're actually buying
auction.lede: Every ad-supported page you open auctions you to dozens of bidders in about a tenth of a second. This is the message that describes you, assembled just now, from your real readings, in the real format (OpenRTB 2.6):
auction.segments: Notice that user.data carries two providers. I could fill the first one: those are interests this page worked out by itself, in milliseconds, with no history and no budget — where you came from, what kind of device this is, whether it's a weekday or a weekend. The confidence field marks which are readings and which are guesses; "high-end device", for one, came out of pixel density, and that is precisely the sort of guess the ad industry treats as fact.
auction.ip: The device.ip field is blank on purpose. A real exchange receives yours; here the IP is read once to find the city and discarded, so there is nothing left to print — and handing someone their own IP back is precisely what this page is objecting to.
auction.segmentPlaceholder: in-market:… — your inferred interests attach here ("in-market for a car", "new parent", "cardholder"). We're not a paying buyer, so we can't show you yours.
auction.brokerGap: The second provider is the one that matters, and it's empty. That's where what you want to buy goes — inferred from your browsing across sites, your purchases, your apps, where you've been. It can't be worked out from a single visit, and it can't be looked up without paying a data broker. So there's the whole asymmetry on one screen: what any page gets for free is up top. What actually sells is just below it, and it's the only part you don't get to see.
